title: Signature Solution - Planning
summary: Students plan a five-part signature solution - goal, prompt structure, inputs, evaluation method and risk plan - and take it through an approve-to-build gate.
objectives: Plan a structured AI solution: state the goal, the prompt structure, and the check steps.
Identify the inputs/data and the output-evaluation method.
Describe one risk and how the plan reduces it.

body: Today you become a designer, not just a prompter. Before anyone types a single word into an AI tool, you will plan a small solution with five parts that fit together: a goal, a prompt structure, inputs, a check, and a risk plan. A good plan is like a bridge design drawn before the first bolt is placed - it lets you find weak spots on paper, where fixing them is cheap.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can state the goal of my solution in one clear sentence.
I can lay out a prompt structure with a role, a task, and one rule.
I can name the inputs my solution needs and how I will check the output.
I can describe one risk and one way my plan reduces it.

terms.definition: A small, reusable AI design with a clear goal and connected parts that solves one simple task.
The shape of a prompt: a role for the AI, a clear task, and at least one rule or limit.
The information a prompt works on, chosen to contain no personal or identifying data.
The agreed way you will judge whether an output is accurate.
A design choice that lowers the chance or impact of something going wrong.

sections.heading: From one prompt to a whole solution
body: In Grade 5 you improved a single prompt. This term you design a solution: a set of parts that work together to do one simple job well.
The five parts are the goal, the [[prompt structure]], the inputs, the [[evaluation method]], and the risk plan. If any part is missing, the solution is harder to trust.

sections.heading: Writing a prompt structure
body: A [[prompt structure]] names a role ('You are a timetable helper'), a task ('list the three earliest buses'), and one rule ('if a time is missing, say so').
The role focuses the AI, the task says exactly what to do, and the rule keeps the output honest and easy to check.

sections.heading: Checks and risks before you build
body: An [[evaluation method]] says how you will judge accuracy, such as comparing the output to a known-correct answer key.

A risk plan names one thing that could go wrong, like a confident wrong answer, and one design choice that reduces it, like a 'say if unsure' rule plus a human check. Never put personal or identifying data into a prompt.

sections.label: Hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: You will now plan your own signature solution on the plan sheet. You will not log in to any tool; the teacher runs any AI on the board. Your job is to make the plan complete and safe.
items: Read your task card and write the goal in one clear sentence.
Fill the role-task-rule slots for your prompt structure.
List the inputs your prompt needs, checking there is no personal data.
Write your evaluation method and one risk with its mitigation.
Self-check against the five-part list, then submit for the approve-to-build gate.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which part of a plan is easiest to forget, and why does that matter?
How does a 'say if unsure' rule make an output safer to trust?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write the one part of your plan you are most confident about.
Write the one part you will strengthen before building next week.

worksheet.title: Week 7 - Core - Worksheet | Signature Solution - Planning

questions.prompt: Name the five parts: using your task card, complete each part of the plan in one line.
questions.stem:
The goal is to ___.
The AI acts as a ___ (role).
The task is to ___.
One rule is ___.
The inputs are ___ (no personal data).
I will check accuracy by ___.
One risk is ___; my plan reduces it by ___.
questions.lookFor: All five parts are present: a goal naming the task and who it helps, a role + task + one rule structure, inputs with no personal or identifying data, a checkable evaluation method (e.g. compare labelled items to a teacher answer key), and one risk with a mitigation that clearly reduces that named risk. Evaluation and risk are the parts most often left blank or thin.

questions.prompt: Spot the weak plan: read the two sample plans provided
questions.lookFor: Chooses the complete plan and names a specific missing part - the evaluation method or the risk row - as the reason, rather than saying the plan is longer or neater. Structure beats size: a missing check is a hidden weak spot.

questions.prompt: My plan review record: fill one row for each of the five parts (plan part / what I wrote / ready? Y/N) and mark whether it is ready.
questions.lookFor: One row per part, each quoting what the student actually wrote plus an honest Y/N. Check the evaluation and risk rows hardest: a 'Y' there should sit beside a method that can really be checked and a mitigation tied to the named risk.

questions.prompt: Exit ticket: write your goal sentence and the one risk your plan reduces.
questions.lookFor: Goal is one clear sentence saying what the solution does and who it helps. The risk is realistic (e.g. a confident but wrong answer) and is one the plan genuinely reduces through its rule, check or human step.

questions.prompt: Challenge (stretch): add a second rule to your prompt structure and explain which kind of wrong answer it is designed to stop.
questions.lookFor: Writes a second rule that fits the same prompt structure and names the kind of wrong answer it blocks (e.g. a confident guess, a dropped item, an unclear label). The link between the rule and the error it stops is what to look for.
